narrative:
FIRST WARN FORECAST
Thursday, September 3, 2026

First. Accurate. Trusted.

EXTREME HEAT WARNING THROUGH SATURDAY EVENING

The prolonged late-season heat wave has reached a more dangerous level across Missouri and Illinois.

The Heat Advisory has been upgraded to an Extreme Heat Warning for the entire First Warn Weather coverage area through Saturday evening. This includes central Missouri, the St. Louis metropolitan area, southeast Missouri, and southern Illinois.

Heat index values Wednesday afternoon reached or exceeded 105 degrees across much of the region, including portions of central Missouri. Similar conditions are expected Thursday, Friday, and Saturday, creating the potential for four consecutive days with heat indices at or above 105 degrees in some locations.

Afternoon temperatures will generally reach the middle to upper 90s, with some locations approaching 100 degrees. Heat index values between 102 and 110 degrees are expected during the afternoon and early evening hours.

The combination of intensity and duration makes this heat wave particularly dangerous.

THURSDAY: DANGEROUS HEAT CONTINUES

A strong upper-level ridge remains firmly established across the central United States, maintaining the unusually hot pattern across Missouri and Illinois.

Temperatures several thousand feet above the surface remain exceptionally warm, while southwest winds and deep atmospheric mixing will allow afternoon temperatures to climb into the middle and upper 90s.

Some locations could again approach 100 degrees.

Humidity remains an important factor. Despite deep mixing Wednesday afternoon, dewpoints only fell into the middle 60s to around 70 degrees. That was enough moisture, combined with temperatures in the upper 90s, to push heat index values above 105 degrees across many locations.

We expect similar conditions today.

Peak heat index values between approximately 102 and 110 degrees are expected during the afternoon and early evening.

There could be a few brief showers, particularly across portions of central Missouri. Similar activity developed Wednesday as the atmosphere briefly became unstable enough to overcome the cap.

However, the strong upper-level ridge will suppress most shower and thunderstorm development. Any activity that manages to develop should be isolated and brief.

Most of the region will remain hot and dry.

FRIDAY: LITTLE TO NO RELIEF

Friday will bring another day of dangerous heat.

There is very little change expected in the overall weather pattern. The upper-level ridge remains in control, temperatures aloft remain extremely warm, and southwest winds continue across the region.

Afternoon temperatures will again reach the middle to upper 90s, with isolated locations potentially nearing 100 degrees.

Heat index values between 102 and 110 degrees will once again be possible.

An isolated shower cannot be completely ruled out, but widespread rainfall is not expected.

By Friday, many communities will have experienced several consecutive days of significant heat. The cumulative effects become increasingly important as a heat wave continues.

Even people who normally tolerate hot weather can experience heat-related illness after repeated exposure without adequate cooling and hydration.

SATURDAY REMAINS DANGEROUSLY HOT

Saturday will likely be the final day of the most intense portion of this heat wave, but it will remain dangerously hot.

High temperatures should once again reach the middle to upper 90s.

A weak cold front will begin approaching from the east later Saturday. Calling it a "cold" front may be somewhat generous, but it should eventually provide at least some relief.

Ahead of the boundary, however, moisture could actually increase slightly. That means heat index values could remain dangerously high even if actual temperatures come down by a degree or two.

There is also a slightly better opportunity for showers or thunderstorms Saturday.

Some computer guidance continues to suggest that a complex of thunderstorms could move southeastward across portions of the Midwest Friday night into Saturday. However, recent trends have shifted the better opportunity farther east.

Only about 15 to 25 percent of our longer-range ensemble guidance currently produces measurable rainfall around St. Louis Saturday.

So while a shower or thunderstorm is possible, widespread rainfall is not expected.

Plan on another dangerously hot day Saturday.

SLIGHT RELIEF SUNDAY

The weak front should move through the region Saturday night.

That will bring some relief Sunday, although the word "cooler" needs some perspective.

High temperatures Sunday will still reach the lower to middle 90s.

Humidity may also remain elevated, with dewpoints potentially remaining in the 70s for portions of the region.

As a result, heat index values could still climb above 100 degrees Sunday, particularly across areas where the front is slower to bring in drier air.

Because of that possibility, some heat-related headlines may eventually need to be extended beyond Saturday evening.

The good news is that the most extreme heat should begin easing.

LABOR DAY REMAINS HOT

Labor Day Monday should bring another small improvement.

High temperatures will still reach the lower to middle 90s, so this will certainly not be a cool holiday.

The difference should be lower humidity.

Dewpoints are expected to fall back into the 60s Monday, which should make conditions feel somewhat more tolerable than what we experience through Saturday.

Anyone with outdoor Labor Day plans should still prepare for significant heat.

Stay hydrated, take frequent breaks, and try to avoid extended strenuous activity during the hottest portion of the afternoon.

Unfortunately, this brief reduction in heat will not last very long.

NEAR-RECORD HEAT RETURNS NEXT WEEK

The upper-level ridge responsible for our current heat wave is expected to rebuild across the region by the middle of next week.

Temperatures will respond quickly.

After the slight reduction Sunday and Labor Day, highs are expected to climb back into the middle and potentially upper 90s by Tuesday and Wednesday.

Some locations could once again approach daily record highs.

This means we may get a short break from the most dangerous heat before another period of significant, potentially near-record warmth develops.

The rebuilding upper-level ridge should also keep widespread rainfall out of the forecast through the middle of next week.

So not only does the heat return, our predominantly dry pattern continues.

EXTREME HEAT SAFETY

An Extreme Heat Warning is more than another hot-weather headline. Conditions over the next several days can produce heat-related illness quickly, especially with prolonged exposure.

Drink plenty of water throughout the day, even if you do not feel thirsty. Avoid strenuous outdoor activity during the hottest part of the afternoon whenever possible.

Outdoor workers should take frequent breaks in air conditioning or shade.

Check on older relatives, friends, neighbors, and anyone without reliable air conditioning.

Remember your pets. Keep plenty of fresh water available, provide shade, and avoid walking dogs on hot pavement during the afternoon.

Never leave a child or animal inside a parked vehicle.

Know the warning signs of heat exhaustion, including heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, nausea, headache, and fainting.

Heat stroke is a medical emergency. Confusion, loss of consciousness, or an extremely high body temperature requires immediate emergency medical attention.

THE BOTTOM LINE

An Extreme Heat Warning is now in effect for the entire First Warn Weather coverage area through Saturday evening.

Thursday, Friday, and Saturday will bring afternoon temperatures in the middle to upper 90s, with some locations approaching 100 degrees.

More importantly, heat index values between 102 and 110 degrees are expected during the afternoon and early evening.

Some communities could experience heat index values at or above 105 degrees for four consecutive days.

A weak cold front should move through Saturday night, providing some relief Sunday and Labor Day. However, highs will still reach the lower to middle 90s, and heat indices could remain above 100 degrees in some locations Sunday.

Labor Day should become somewhat less humid as drier air arrives.

Then temperatures begin climbing again.

Another period of significant and potentially near-record heat is expected by the middle of next week as the upper-level ridge rebuilds across Missouri and Illinois.

We are now dealing with a prolonged and dangerous late-season heat wave. Take the Extreme Heat Warning seriously, limit prolonged exposure during the afternoon, stay hydrated, and check on those who may be particularly vulnerable to the heat.

severeNarrative:
First Warn Forecast & Severe Weather Outlook Update
11:50 AM CDT | Wednesday, June 17, 2026
First Warn Weather Alert Day
Headlines
Severe thunderstorms remain likely this afternoon and evening across Missouri and Illinois.
Damaging winds up to 85 mph, large hail up to 2.5 inches, and several tornadoes remain possible.
The greatest threat locally remains across eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois, including the St. Louis metro area.
Strong southwest winds will gust between 40 and 50 mph outside of thunderstorms.
Peak severe weather threat for the St. Louis area remains between 6 PM and 9 PM.

A potentially dangerous severe weather outbreak remains on track across portions of Missouri and Illinois this afternoon and evening. There has been little change in the overall forecast since this morning. The Storm Prediction Center continues to highlight much of eastern and central Missouri and western Illinois in an Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5) for severe weather, while portions of central Illinois remain under a Moderate Risk (Level 4 of 5) where the highest threat for significant severe weather exists.

An intense cluster of thunderstorms that developed overnight across Iowa produced wind gusts exceeding 90 mph and continues to influence the forecast across Illinois late this morning. The primary outflow boundary currently extends from far northeast Missouri into portions of south-central Illinois. This boundary will likely serve as a focus for severe thunderstorm development later today.

Strong sunshine south of the boundary is allowing temperatures to rapidly climb through the 80s while dew points remain in the upper 60s and lower 70s. Combined with an exceptionally strong wind field aloft, conditions remain favorable for supercells capable of producing all severe weather hazards.

While morning storms may slightly alter where the greatest risk ultimately develops, confidence remains high that numerous severe thunderstorms will develop this afternoon and continue through the evening hours.

Primary Threats

🌪 Several Tornadoes Possible

A few strong tornadoes remain possible.
Greatest tornado threat remains across central Illinois.
Tornadoes remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois, especially near any lingering outflow boundaries.

💨 Destructive Winds Possible

Widespread damaging winds of 60 to 80 mph.
Isolated wind gusts exceeding 85 mph remain possible.
Significant tree damage and widespread power outages could occur.

🧊 Large to Very Large Hail

Large hail remains possible with discrete supercells.
Hailstones up to 2.5 inches in diameter may occur.
Timing Across Missouri and Illinois
1 PM - 3 PM

The first severe thunderstorms are expected to develop across northeast Missouri and portions of west-central Illinois. Areas near Quincy, Kirksville, Palmyra, Hannibal, and surrounding communities should closely monitor conditions.

3 PM - 6 PM

The severe weather threat expands southeast into central Missouri and western Illinois. Columbia, Jefferson City, Mexico, Bowling Green, Troy, and portions of the northern St. Louis metro could see supercells capable of producing tornadoes, very large hail, and destructive winds.

6 PM - 9 PM

This remains the peak severe weather window for the St. Louis metropolitan area and much of eastern Missouri and western Illinois. Storms may become more widespread during this period while maintaining the potential to produce damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes. Residents from St. Louis and St. Charles to Edwardsville, Belleville, Alton, Farmington, and surrounding communities should be prepared to act quickly if warnings are issued.

9 PM - Midnight

Storms are expected to organize into a line extending from central Missouri into southern Indiana. Damaging straight-line winds become the primary threat as storms shift into southeast Missouri and southern Illinois. Heavy rainfall and localized flooding may also develop overnight.

Local First Warn Outlook

The highest confidence for severe weather today exists across the Enhanced Risk area covering much of eastern and central Missouri, including Columbia, Jefferson City, the St. Louis metro, northeast Missouri, and west-central Illinois.

Farther south, a Slight Risk extends across southern Missouri and southern Illinois, including Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon. Severe thunderstorms remain possible in these areas, but storm coverage and intensity may be somewhat lower than locations farther north.

The lowest severe weather threat remains across the Missouri Bootheel and far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border where a Marginal Risk remains in place. However, isolated severe storms cannot be ruled out.

Threat Levels

Central Illinois
Areas northeast of Springfield, Illinois
Greatest potential for strong tornadoes and destructive winds

🟤 Enhanced Risk (Level 3 of 5)

Central Missouri
Eastern Missouri
St. Louis Metro
West-central Illinois
Southwest Illinois

🟡 Slight Risk (Level 2 of 5)

Southern Missouri
South-central Missouri
Southeast Missouri
Southern Illinois
Rolla, Salem, Farmington, Fredericktown, Marion, and Mount Vernon

🟢 Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 5)

Missouri Bootheel
Far southern Illinois near the Kentucky border
Areas south of Poplar Bluff and near Paducah
Additional Concern: Strong Winds Outside of Storms

Even outside of thunderstorms, strong southwest winds will continue through the afternoon. Sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph with gusts of 40 to 50 mph are expected. Loose outdoor objects should be secured, and travel may become difficult for high-profile vehicles.

Thursday Outlook

The cold front responsible for today's severe weather will gradually move south of the region overnight. Showers and a few thunderstorms may linger into Thursday, especially across southeast Missouri and southwest Illinois. Cooler temperatures in the 70s and lower 80s will provide a welcome break from today's heat and humidity.

Bottom Line

There has been little change in the forecast thinking since this morning. The atmosphere remains primed for severe thunderstorm development this afternoon and evening. While the greatest threat for strong tornadoes remains across central Illinois, all severe weather hazards remain possible across eastern Missouri and western Illinois.

The St. Louis metro remains in the corridor for severe weather between 6 PM and 9 PM, with damaging winds, large hail, and tornadoes all possible. Everyone across the First Warn viewing area should remain weather aware and have multiple ways to receive warnings throughout the day and tonight.

First Warn Weather: First. Accurate. Trusted.
